passage: Note by Minakshi, seminar supervisor. Farhan presented his final-year project on Tuesday. Halfway through he lost a word and apologised twice. Afterwards I overheard him in the corridor listing "all the mistakes" to a classmate: the pause, the mispronounced name, the missing slide number. I had noticed only the pause. I asked what he thought the audience remembered. "That I froze." I read him my notes: three points about his results and one question from the panel. Nothing about the name. Farhan laughed, relieved but not fully convinced. At the next seminar I will ask two classmates what they remembered. - Minakshi

qa.q: Which three mistakes did Farhan list in the corridor?
qa.a: Farhan listed the pause, the mispronounced name and the missing slide number.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling after the seminar?
qa.a: Embarrassed and anxious, believing everyone had noticed each slip.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do to help Farhan see the talk differently?
qa.a: Minakshi asked what the audience remembered and read out the notes, which held results and a panel question but nothing about the name.

qa.q: What did Minakshi's notes show about how the audience saw the talk?
qa.a: They noticed the pause and the results, but not the mispronounced name, so attention stayed on the content.

grounding: Shows a student who believes every stumble was noticed while an observer's notes show far less was noticed.

passage: Thursday night. Viva done. I said "thermodynamical" instead of "thermodynamic" and lost my thread on slide six for about ten seconds. I replayed both all evening. Then Hansa texted: "Great viva! The sensor part was so clear." I asked, "Did you notice slide six?" "Which slide six? I was panicking about my own viva tomorrow." I laughed out loud. Hansa had not heard the word or the pause, and only remembered the sensor part. So maybe people are busy with their own heads. I'm still cringing a little, but less. - Tejas

qa.q: Which two slips did Tejas replay all evening?
qa.a: Tejas replayed saying "thermodynamical" and losing the thread on slide six for about ten seconds.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling as the evening went on?
qa.a: Embarrassed and self-critical, cringing at the two slips.

qa.q: What did Tejas learn by asking Hansa about slide six?
qa.a: That Hansa had not noticed the slip and was busy with Hansa's own viva, so audiences notice less than a speaker fears.

qa.q: What was Hansa thinking about during Tejas's viva?
qa.a: Hansa was panicking about Hansa's own viva the next day and remembered mainly the clear sensor part.

grounding: Shows a student replaying small stumbles while a listener remembers almost nothing of them.

passage:
Supervisor's note, final-year seminar series, week 6.
Sudha presented her project on rainwater harvesting today. It was well organised. About four minutes in, she said "catchment" wrongly, paused, corrected it and went on. The rest was confident.
Afterwards she came to my desk looking close to tears. "Everyone heard that. They'll remember it as the girl who can't say 'catchment.'"
I asked her to wait. When the class returned from the break, I asked them, without naming anyone, to write down one thing they remembered from each talk. On Sudha's, eleven of fourteen wrote about the rooftop tank photo. Nobody mentioned the word. Rekha, who presented after her, wrote only "I was too nervous about mine to notice much."
I showed Sudha the slips. She read them twice and let out a long breath.
I will repeat this exercise with the next group; it helps.
— Seminar supervisor

qa.q: What did most of the class remember about Sudha's talk?
qa.a: Eleven of fourteen wrote about the rooftop tank photo.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she came to the desk?
qa.a: Sudha was upset and ashamed, close to tears and sure everyone had noticed and would remember the mistake.

qa.q: Which choice by the supervisor worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking the class to write what they remembered, because it showed Sudha real evidence that the stumble went unnoticed.

qa.q: What was the seminar like for Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha was too nervous about her own talk to notice much about Sudha's.

grounding: Shows a student sure that a small stumble was noticed and remembered, and evidence that the audience noticed far less.

passage:
Thursday night.
Viva today. First question, easy. Second question, I said "resistance" when I meant "resistor." The external examiner raised one eyebrow, I corrected myself, and we moved on.
I have replayed that eyebrow maybe fifty times since. I'm sure the examiner wrote it down. I'm sure Samir, who was waiting by the door, heard. By dinner I had decided that everyone in the lab now thinks I don't know basic circuits.
Then I actually asked Samir. He looked blank. "What mistake?" He'd been standing there going over his own answers in his head, terrified about the transistor question.
Also: my marks are up on the portal. Good grade.
So the whole lab was not thinking about me. The examiner had probably seen that slip a hundred times. Everyone was busy with their own nerves.
Note to self, Kashish: next viva, correct it and move on. Nobody's keeping a list.

qa.q: What word did the narrator say instead of "resistor"?
qa.a: The narrator said "resistance."

qa.q: How did Kashish feel in the hours after the viva?
qa.a: Kashish felt anxious and embarrassed, replaying the examiner's eyebrow about fifty times.

qa.q: What did Kashish learn to do next time?
qa.a: Correct the slip and move on, remembering that listeners notice far less than it feels.

qa.q: What was Samir focused on while waiting by the door?
qa.a: Samir was terrified about his own transistor question and going over his answers, so he never noticed the slip.

grounding: Illustrates a student sure that a small slip in a viva was noticed by everyone, and finding others were busy with their own nerves.

passage:
Sarika: I'm never showing my face in class again
Yamini: what?? the seminar was good
Sarika: my hands were SHAKING
Sarika: and I skipped a slide and had to go back
Sarika: everyone saw
Yamini: I honestly didn't notice the slide thing
Sarika: you're just being nice
Yamini: no really. I was going over my own intro the whole time. I was next 😬
Yamini: what I remember is your graph with the two lines. that was clear
Sarika: …the graph?
Yamini: yes. Tanya said the same after
Sarika: I thought everyone was looking at my hands
Yamini: most people are thinking about their own turn. or lunch
Sarika: ok that's weirdly comforting
Yamini: go eat something. you did fine 🙂

qa.q: What does Yamini remember from Sarika's seminar?
qa.a: Your graph with the two lines.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel right after the seminar?
qa.a: Sarika felt embarrassed and anxious, sure that everyone saw the shaking hands and the skipped slide.

qa.q: How did Yamini help Sarika see the seminar more accurately?
qa.a: Yamini said honestly what was noticed and what was not, and pointed out that most people were thinking about their own turn.

qa.q: Why did Yamini not notice the skipped slide?
qa.a: Yamini was nervous about the intro that came next, being the next speaker.

grounding: Shows a student who believes every stumble was seen, and a friend who reveals the audience noticed far less.

passage: At the agricultural college in Hassan, Dhruv's seminar on drip irrigation was the last of the afternoon, with twenty classmates and three farmers from the demonstration plot on the benches. Halfway through, he dropped the wooden pointer with a clatter, said "drop irrigation" instead of "drip", and lost his place for what felt like a full minute. His ears burned. He finished, sat down and replayed it: the clatter, the word, the silence. Everyone must think he was a fool. On the bus home he finally asked Raghav, "How bad was the pointer thing?" Raghav looked blank. "What pointer thing?" "I dropped it. And said drop irrigation." "Did you? I was busy worrying about my own slides. The tank diagram was good, though. That old farmer asked you about the pipes after, na?" Dhruv stared out at the coconut groves. The farmer had asked. Nobody had asked about the pointer.

qa.q: What did Dhruv say instead of "drip irrigation"?
qa.a: "Drop irrigation".

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel after sitting down?
qa.a: Dhruv was embarrassed and anxious, ears burning, replaying the stumble and sure everyone thought he was a fool.

qa.q: What could Dhruv remind himself before his next seminar?
qa.a: That listeners notice far less than he fears, as Raghav's blank look showed, and that they remember the useful parts like the tank diagram.

qa.q: How did Raghav experience Dhruv's seminar?
qa.a: Raghav barely noticed the stumble, being busy worrying about his own slides, and remembered the good tank diagram and the farmer's question instead.

grounding: Shows a student sure that every small stumble in his seminar was noticed, while the audience was mostly thinking about itself.
